verdicts.why: A's mark is a trunk with a felling notch and root flare, drawn from the arborist's own work. It is a solid, simple silhouette that stays the same shape at 32 and 16 px and works in one color, cut vinyl and embroidery. B's tree-ring disc with a wedge cut is a more familiar category motif and can read as a power or refresh icon. Its thin concentric rings blur together at 16 px, and its reversed version changes the figure-ground of the center rather than simply inverting it. Both spell the name correctly and add nothing. A's condensed wordmark with tracked TREE CARE is the more deliberate lockup, while B uses a default-looking bold sans.

Both spell the name exactly and add nothing invented, and both marks hold their shape at 16 and 32 px and in one color and reversed. B's mark is a trunk with a felling notch cut into it, which comes straight from an arborist's work and isn't a green tree in a circle; A's notched ring reads more like a generic 'C', a camera or a power icon, so the tree-ring idea gets lost. B's lockup also looks more deliberate (a condensed ironwood-weight wordmark over widely spaced TREE CARE), while A pairs its mark with a default-looking bold sans, though B's small spaced line will need care when embroidered.

A's BR monogram fails in one color and reversed: the letters disappear and leave a blank rounded square. That breaks the brief's one-ink stamp and embroidery use. B's split disc stays the same bold shape at 16 px, in one ink and reversed, with no thin parts, and its serif wordmark sets the full name correctly. B's mark is generic and could pass for a coffee bean or any horizon emblem, but A's default-looking condensed sans in a rounded app-icon box is no more distinctive and fails the more important survival test.

B's mark breaks in one ink and reversed: the BR letters are knocked out in a second color, so the one-color and reversed versions turn into a blank rounded square. That fails the brief's single-ink stamp on kraft bags and its embroidery. A's split disc stays solid and recognizable at 16 px, in one ink and reversed, and its serif wordmark is set cleanly. Its one weakness is a generic idea: it vaguely suggests a horizon or dark water but could belong to anyone, as could B's monogram in a rounded box, so B gains nothing on concept.

A has the more distinctive palette for this brewery: Kettle Copper, River Blue and Barley Gold, each with a clear job. Its contrast table is complete, it has responsible-drinking rules for photos, and its can-label compliance note is useful. B's palette is almost all green and cream, its 'Cream on Green' swatch is shown as cream on cream, its footer lists 'logo.svg, logo.svg', and its tagline capitalizes 'Locals' by mistake. A's weak spot is that the logo misuse items (stretch, skew, recolor) are missing a 'Don't' label, while B's imagery rules are more specific.

A sticks strictly to the brief, and its voice and imagery rules are specific and easy to apply: the bank building, Erik and Nils at work with their permission, no fake grain or sepia filters, no AI-redrawn lettering. B has the more distinctive palette, adding copper, river blue and gold, and a useful note on federal alcohol labeling. But B adds details the brief doesn't support, such as a stone facade and a designated-driver promise, and its logo misuse list has no 'don't' label, so 'Stretch, skew, or rotate' reads as an instruction. A has its own flaws: an almost entirely green-and-cream palette with two swatches sharing the same hex, the logo filename printed twice in the footer, and a logo variant too small to read. Still, A is the safer guide to hand to staff.

verdicts.why: A gives each of its eight colors a hex value and a clear role, says outright that coral is not for text, and backs that with a contrast table. Its three voice principles each have a Do and a Don't example aimed at nervous adults and toddlers, and the teal-plus-coral palette is more distinctive. B uses a cold, generic teal-and-gray palette and shows no sample of its body typeface. B's picture rules list the things to avoid in an unlabeled column, so they read like rules to follow, and 'close enough to see the tool' works against calming nervous patients. Neither guide invents facts, but A is more complete and more useful at the front desk.

Neither page invents facts, and both give hex values with clear roles and contrast ratios. B is the more useful system for this client: it adds a warm coral accent to the usual dental teal and explains which shade is safe for text. Its three voice principles each come with a do and a don't written for nervous adults and toddlers, and its imagery rules are specific enough to judge a photo (no drills or open mouths in first-visit images, written consent, faces at eye level). A is clean and well built, but its all-teal palette is generic for the category, and its two picture columns have no labels, so it's unclear which one lists the things to avoid. B's leftover placeholder 'Clear space = N cap height' and its small 11–13 px body sizes keep the margin slight.

A invents three street names that aren't in the brief (Elm St. & Birch Ln., Hollis Ct., Walnut Ave.). The facts criterion treats that as a serious fault, even though A's route timeline and offline 'last seen here' treatment are richer. B shows exactly the brief's content: 3 stops away, about 6 minutes, Oak St. and Ridgeway Ave., and Mr. Dorsey. Its offline state labels the data as last known and gives a clear 'Try again' action. B is weaker on craft: the route card has a lot of empty space, the status bar is generic, and A's offline footer slightly overlaps its card. These are minor next to A's made-up content.

B makes up three intermediate stop names (Elm St. & Birch Ln., Hollis Ct., Walnut Ave.) that the brief never gives, which is a serious factual fault in a tracker parents rely on. A shows the same three-stops-away route as unnamed stops and invents nothing, and its offline state clearly says 'No connection. Last update 2 minutes ago', labels the bus as 'Last known position' and gives a clear 'Try again' action. B is more polished and handles staleness well (grayed values, a dashed 'last seen' marker), but its invented stops and the offline footer crowding the route card outweigh that.

A's prominent 'Check in remaining (2)' bulk button invites skipping the per-animal tag and papers check the brief requires. The brief says the volunteer checks in each animal after seeing its tag and health papers. A builds that into the screen: each animal has an 'Ear tag and health papers checked' box, and its check-in button stays inactive until the box is ticked. B's main action, 'Check in remaining (2)', checks in several animals with one tap and skips that check. verdicts.why: Both spell the name exactly and invent nothing. B's blocky pixel mark stays crisp at 16 px, but it reads more like an airplane or antenna than a tree, and it sits next to a default bold sans with no lockup design, so it's ambiguous and has no craft. A's shield-and-branch is a deliberate, balanced lockup with a strong serif and spaced caps that suits a certified-arborist trade. Its shield silhouette and stem still hold up at 32 and 16 px and in one color and reversed, though the thin inner line would need dropping for embroidery and the hard-hat sticker.

Both spell the name correctly and add nothing, so survival decides: A's chunky blocky tree keeps exactly the same shape at 32 and 16 px and in one color and reversed. B's shield-and-branch turns to grey mush at 16 px, and its thin inner gold outline, hairline rule and tiny tracked 'TREE CARE' would vanish when embroidered or cut in vinyl. B is the more polished drawing, but both rely on a generic tree, and A's crude mark and default bold sans make this a narrow win.

Neither sheet invents anything, and both spell the name correctly. B's solid, notched B is the same clear shape at 32 and 16 px and holds up in one ink, reversed, stamped and embroidered. A's waterfall idea is closer to the client's own subject, while B's mark is only a generic initial set beside a default-looking serif, but survival at small sizes ranks higher and decides it.

A's heavy solid B keeps the same shape at 32 and 16 px and will stamp, embroider and reverse cleanly; B's thin outlined B with water lines and a zigzag turns to gray mush at 16 px, and its hairline strokes and rule under BLACKWATER would disappear on kraft stamping or embroidery. B's water and ridge idea is closer to the client's own subject than A's plain monogram with its notched counters, but that does not make up for it failing at small sizes.

Neither guide invents anything: both stick to the brief's facts. B is the more usable handoff. It has logo clear-space and do-not-crop rules, a full contrast table, named fonts (Fraunces and Work Sans) with a size scale, voice examples set out as Say/Not pairs taken from real brief details, and imagery Do/Don't lists specific enough to judge a photo against. A has a bolder poster-style layout and good voice cards, but it gives no logo usage rules, and its imagery and type guidance are thinner. B loses some ground for small slips: the footer lists logo.svg twice, Bank Plaster and Warm Chalk share the same hex, and the ochre logo tile is too small to read.

Both guides stick to the brief's facts. They give hex values with clear roles and name their type pairing and sizes. B has a more distinctive system for this client: a bold Oswald and Source Sans pairing, a Quarry Rust accent with a large-type-only rule, and four voice cards with Do/Don't lines that sound like the taproom, plus a footer that puts the key facts in front of staff. A has a thorough contrast table, but it is let down by craft slips: two swatches share the same hex (#fffcf4 is listed as both Bank Plaster and Warm Chalk), the footer reads 'logo.svg, logo.svg', and the ochre logo tile is too small to read, so the page feels more like a template.
